documents.abstract: Introduction Industrial exoskeletons with integrated sensors are emerging as a technology for monitoring biomechanical exposure and supporting the prevention of work-related musculoskeletal disorders in industrial environments. Methods This systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, retrieving 106 studies published between 2021 and 2026 from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. VOSviewer version 1.6.20 and R‐Studio version 2026.01.2+418 were used for bibliometric and descriptive analyses. The review provides a qualitative synthesis supported by descriptive quantitative reporting of the extracted outcomes. Results The evidence indicated a technological shift from passive devices toward intelligent exoskeletons integrating surface electromyography, inertial measurement units, machine vision, physiological sensors, and artificial intelligence. Individual studies reported maximum reductions of 68.2% in muscle activity, 34% in spinal compression, and up to 60% in muscle fatigue, alongside productivity improvements of up to 59.5%. Machine learning approaches achieved an ROC of 0.985, automated assessment accuracies of 98.5%, and posture estimation with an ICC of 0.967. However, these values were not pooled estimates and varied across study designs, sensor configurations, tasks, and assessment protocols. Discussion The evidence remains constrained by small sample sizes, sensor drift, interoperability limitations, and insufficient long‐term validation in real‐world industrial environments. Sensor‐integrated exoskeletons show potential for ergonomic monitoring and risk reduction, but their effectiveness and industrial generalizability require further validation through standardized, interoperable, and longitudinal field studies.

We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests. Using this benchmark, the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively). Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The traditional methods for fusing images acquired under low-light conditions, in many cases, are unable to retain sufficient integrity of structural and textural features, resulting in a distorted and degraded ability to detect features within a scene. This paper presents a novel approach to overcome these issues by using Spiking Graph Explainable Artificial Intelligence (SGXAI) with Fire Hawk Optimization (FHO) to effectively fuse infrared and visible image data. This new SGXAI_FHO framework uses a combination of Gaussian smoothing algorithms to reduce image noise, brightness, and contrast enhancement techniques on visible images to improve the image quality perceived by the human eye (the observer), as well as cross-modal attention (CMA) mechanisms to extract complementary features from the two input modalities and to prioritize these features during the fusion process. The results of this experimentation provide compelling evidence of the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed framework, achieving an F1-score of 99.81%, precision of 99.46%, recall of 99.72%, and accuracy of 99.56%. These results demonstrate that the SGXAI_FHO framework will provide a robust, reliable, and interpretable approach for low-light image fusion and detection applications and has substantial potential for real-world applications.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are increasingly embedded in educational systems, yet their implications for self-regulated learning (SRL) and metacognitive development remain only partially understood. This study conducts a systematic literature review of 34 empirical and review articles investigating AI-driven learning analytics in formal education settings, focusing on their impact on SRL, motivation, and academic performance. Following PRISMA-aligned procedures, the review identifies studies involving AI-based analytics tools, standardized SRL or metacognitive assessments, and empirical designs with pre–post or comparison data. The results indicate that AI-driven systems such as predictive models, adaptive platforms, chatbots, and generative AI can strengthen core SRL processes, increase motivation and engagement, and improve academic outcomes across diverse subjects and educational levels. However, the review also reveals persistent implementation challenges, including infrastructural limitations, teacher preparedness, privacy and ethical issues, and potential over-reliance on AI that may weaken independent strategic thinking. The article concludes that AI-driven learning analytics can meaningfully support SRL when embedded within coherent pedagogical frameworks and supported by institutional policies, and it outlines directions for future research on mechanisms, equity, and long-term effects.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: People prefer deliberation to intuition, when judging how others solve hard problems, and they extend this to artificial agents. Yet in the moral domain, the preference may reverse as intuitive moral responses appear to signal good character. One explanation is that fast, intuitive responses show real emotional engagement. Since machines are thought to lack emotion, it is unclear whether a preference for intuition in the moral domain extends to AI. Across three preregistered studies (N = 2,173), we find that it does, but that it appears to be driven by commitment to moral norms and precedents rather than emotion. In Study 1, participants preferred intuitive reasoning for moral decisions and systematic reasoning for non-moral decisions, for human and AI agents alike. Intuitive moral reasoning signalled better character but was not clearly expected to produce better outcomes. In Study 2, the character preference persisted when the AI was described as being incapable of emotion. In Study 3, we held the decision fixed and varied how firmly the agent held the relevant moral norm. An agent who would never reconsider applying a moral norm was rated above one who would reconsider given sufficiently high stakes; and both above one who weighed costs and benefits case by case. Commitment raised character ratings more than expected-outcome ratings. The character-based cost of moral deliberation appears to be a cost of treating a moral norm as negotiable, and we found strong evidence that people apply this inference to machines and people alike.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: Silicon sampling generates survey respondents by having a large language model (LLM) answer a survey as a person with given demographic attributes, and the resulting synthetic populations are increasingly used in place of human ones. Existing evaluations focus on individual-answer accuracy, per-question answer distributions, and correlations across questions. None of these compares the respondents themselves, so a generator whose respondents have combinations of answers found in no human respondent can still score well if it reproduces every answer distribution. We propose the respondent coverage gap (RCG), which represents each respondent as a point defined by their complete answer profile and measures how far each human respondent is from the nearest generated one, relative to the distance between human samples. On two US social surveys, all six LLMs we evaluate leave human respondents uncovered, and under our main settings, they fall behind a baseline that samples each answer independently from the human marginals. Across the prompting and inference settings we test, every LLM has a higher RCG than a Gaussian copula fitted to the human data.

Background Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare, high-acuity perioperative emergency requiring coordinated crisis resource management (CRM). Limited clinical exposure has made simulation-based education central to developing and sustaining CRM competency among perioperative teams. Methods An integrative review guided by the Whittemore and Knafl framework and PRISMA standards searched EMBASE, Scopus, CINAHL, and MEDLINE (October 2025-March 2026). Twenty-seven peer-reviewed publications examining simulation-based CRM and MH management in interprofessional perioperative teams met inclusion criteria. Results Simulation outperformed non-simulation modalities in developing technical and nontechnical skills and team coordination. Structured debriefing drove learning and skills transfer more than active participation. Skills decayed within months without reinforcement but were mitigated by longitudinal and just-in-time training. Cognitive load and human factors frameworks explained performance breakdown and persistent knowledge gaps, and inconsistent readiness emerged as an ongoing patient concern. Conclusion Simulation-based education coupled with structured debriefing and longitudinal reinforcement builds and sustains CRM competency for MH and other perioperative crises. Continuous investment in recurring training, competency assessment, and institutional readiness is needed to translate competence into effective team performance and improved patient outcomes.

Evaluation of facial skin parameters is important for accurate diagnosis and computerized systems can reduce subjectivity. We evaluated the feasibility of an application-based facial analysis artificial intelligence (AI) system by comparing its output to a human dermatologist evaluator. Both an application-based AI and human dermatologist assessed the severity of 14 parameters (age spots, eye bags, moisture, oiliness, redness, texture, wrinkles, acne, droopy lower eyelid, droopy upper eyelid, firmness, dark circles, radiance, pores). The AI generated a raw score between 0 and 100 (100 = flawless) that was converted to match the human rating between 0 and 4 (4 = very severe). Differences in ratings were calculated to determine the degree of agreement. A 0-point difference is defined as complete agreement, a 1-point difference is good, a 2-point difference is poor, a 3-point difference is very poor, and a 4-point difference is worst. In total, 46 facial clinical photos (13 male, 33 female) taken indoors under fluorescent lighting with and without flash were assessed. Parameters with high rates (> 90%) of complete or good agreement were redness (100%), eye bags (96%), and wrinkles (96%). Parameters with moderate rates (80–90%) of agreement were radiance (89%), dark circles (84%), droopy lower eyelid (82%), oiliness (80%), acne (80%), and pores (80%). Parameters with low rates (< 80%) of agreement were texture (78%), age spots (78%), droopy upper eyelid (77%), moisture (72%), and firmness (65%). In a preliminary study of one neural-network AI, its evaluation of skin parameters had an 83% overall complete or good agreement with a human rater. While software-based AI facial analysis systems may lack hardware optimization, they are simple to use and convenient to implement on a variety of hand-held devices. Low start-up costs, rapid data collection, and easy use can be advantages over higher cost, desktop-based facial analysis devices.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Food cold chains are increasingly instrumented with connected temperature sensors, intelligent packaging, product-quality measurements and predictive algorithms. Yet the transition from monitoring refrigeration conditions to managing actual product deterioration is neither automatic nor equally reliable across commodities. This critical narrative review evaluates how sensing, multimodal data fusion, artificial intelligence and remaining shelf-life models can support decisions throughout refrigerated food supply chains. Peer-reviewed work published from 2000 to 12 August 2026 was considered, alongside selected foundational studies, through accessible scholarly indexes, bibliographic verification and backward citation examination. Evidence was assessed for biological relevance, measurement validity, independent validation, operational deployment and decision-level consequences. Temperature histories provide an essential but incomplete representation of product condition: packaging atmosphere, initial microbiological or physiological state, humidity, mechanical injury and spatial thermal gradients can materially affect deterioration. Laboratory studies demonstrate promising performance for electronic noses, spectroscopy, flexible indicators and machine-learning models, whereas external route-level validation and calibration across product lots remain comparatively limited. Kinetic models offer interpretable relationships between exposure and quality loss but depend on commodity-specific parameters and assumptions; data-driven models can represent complex patterns but are vulnerable to distribution shift and leakage between training and test samples. Digital-twin and remaining-life allocation studies establish plausible pathways towards first-expired-first-out distribution, yet simulated reductions in waste should not be mistaken for demonstrated commercial benefits. A central distinction is made between marketable quality and microbiological safety: freshness estimates cannot independently establish pathogen absence, extend legally defined use-by dates or replace food-safety controls. The review proposes an uncertainty-aware sequence linking measurement, state estimation, validated remaining-life prediction and constrained operational action. Research priorities include prospective multi-site studies, robust ground truth, calibration transfer, human–algorithm decision trials and transparent accounting of energy, waste and equity. Smart cold chains are best understood as governed decision systems rather than collections of sensors or predictive models.
topics: Postharvest Quality and Shelf Life Management

documents.abstract: Online learning platforms provide access to educational content, but many systems deliver the same material to every learner andoffer limited support for identifying individual learning needs. This paper proposes a Smart E-Learning Platform using ArtificialIntelligence (AI) that aims to personalize learning through learner profiles, progress tracking, recommendation methods,automated practice feedback, and a dashboard for learners and instructors. The proposed workflow collects learning activity andassessment results, processes relevant learning indicators, and recommends suitable resources or practice activities. Possible AImethods include rule-based recommendation as a baseline, content-based filtering, and supervised models when sufficientlabelled data is available. The platform is designed as an academic prototype and should be evaluated using measurableindicators such as recommendation relevance, task completion, learner satisfaction, and usability. No implementation results orimprovement percentages are claimed in this proposal. Privacy, transparency, accessibility, and instructor oversight areimportant requirements. The system is intended to support teaching and learning, not to replace teachers or make high-stakesdecisions about students
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Global climate change has affected different factors of society, including agriculture, which is one of the key income factors for a country’s economy. Reports predicting the increase in the human population by 2050 have alerted us to the increase in demand in food production required to support this population. This demand can be achieved before 2050 by a hybrid of traditional agricultural practices blended with technology for sustainable agriculture, soil moisture, plant health, pest control, water management, etc. As water scarcity in some regions has risen due to climate change, efficient water management is critical. These systems combine artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation with precise real-time sensing. This chapter highlights the value and implications of smart irrigation for effective and sustainable farming methods, which is fueled by nanosensors and Internet of Things technologies. Because they track pH and moisture levels and help with nutrient availability, nanosensors are essential to smart irrigation, allowing farmers to apply fertilizer and water more effectively. Such sensors are biodegradable and uses cloud servers and wireless communication to transmit data to the Internet of Things. An automated system that considers the unique requirements of each crop, weather patterns, and soil health is used to process and analyze the data. This system also automatically starts irrigation without human intervention. Proper water management and soil health can promote sustainability and yield crop growth.
topics: Innovations in Aquaponics and Hydroponics Systems

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and digital automation technologies have transformed residential environments from conventional living spaces into intelligent ecosystems capable of responding to users’ safety, comfort, and lifestyle requirements. Traditionally, residential security systems were primarily dependent on mechanical locks, physical surveillance, and human monitoring. However, contemporary smart security systems integrate biometric authentication, intelligent surveillance, automated access control, sensor-based monitoring, and cloud-connected platforms to create responsive and adaptive residential environments. This review paper explores the integration of smart security and access control systems within residential interior design projects through a case study approach. The study examines how technological interventions influence spatial planning, material selection, user interaction, and aesthetic considerations in modern residential interiors. A qualitative review methodology is adopted by analysing existing research, technological frameworks, and representative residential applications. The paper evaluates major components including smart locks, biometric systems, video doorbells, motion sensors, AI-enabled cameras, integrated home automation platforms, and cybersecurity mechanisms. The study proposes an integrated design framework demonstrating how security technologies can be embedded within residential interiors without compromising visual quality and spatial experience. The findings indicate that successful implementation requires collaboration between interior designers, architects, technology consultants, and homeowners during early design stages. The paper highlights that future residential interior will increasingly depend on invisible, intelligent, and user-centred security systems where safety becomes an integrated design feature rather than an independent technological addition.

In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation. We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92). We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.

The advent and rapid spread of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative Artificial Intelligencesystems have marked an epistemological and structural discontinuity in the Information Society.While the early phases of the digital transition were characterized by processes of digitization, indexing,and heuristic data retrieval — where the machine acted primarily as an archivist or intermediary towardprimary content —, the current configuration of algorithmic architecture responds to a qualitativelydifferent dynamic. Artificial Intelligence does not merely organize human knowledge; to function,learn its semantic structures, and provide real-time synthesis, it requires the continuous, massive, andsystematic assimilation of informational material produced by humanity.To describe this phenomenon of insatiable and structural nourishment, we propose here the analyticalcategory of «infofagia» (derived from the Greek root phagêin, "to eat", combined with the informationalprefix). AI infofagia does not constitute a mere computational phase of the machine — the technicalphase of training on datasets —, but rather a total sociological and psychological fact. It identifies anextractive and metabolic process in which humanity's entire cultural, scientific, artistic, andconversational production is converted into raw matter, "ingested" by mathematical models, digested,and finally returned in the form of synthetic and normalized output.Adopting the paradigm of infofagia allows us to overcome both purely deterministic readings oftechnology and apologetic visions tied to the alleged democratization of knowledge. Through theanalysis of empirical data, international case studies, and clinical-social feedback, this essaydemonstrates how the informational appetite of large algorithmic models is not neutral, but directlyretroacts upon economic structures, cultural diversity, and the psyche of the final consumer.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is turning the older digital divide of the developing world into an intelligence-economy participation divide: an asymmetry in the capacity of states to shape, own, govern and draw value from cognitive automation. Read against the literatures on digital colonialism, data extractivism and the "Data Nullius" framework, this article treats Sovereign AI as a distinct policy object for the Global South rather than a subset of digital public infrastructure or industrial policy. It sets out four interlocking registers of sovereignty (compute, supply chain, model and data) and argues for a modular, developmental architecture governed through "fluid institutionalism", built on the principle of foundations before the frontier: connectivity, device affordability and FAIR-aligned digital public infrastructure first, then retrieval-grounded small language models. The article then examines whole-of-government interoperability and tiered human-in-the-loop governance; economic transformation through public procurement; security resilience through inbound and outbound data embassies; local-language models such as Bhashini and InkubaLM; a "choose partners, not sides" posture in a bipolar technology rivalry; and South-South cooperation for a stronger voice in global AI governance. It closes with the binding constraints of energy, water, fiscal capacity and coordination, an assessment of risks including dependency lock-in, elite capture and linguistic exclusion, and a time-phased set of recommendations by institutional actor.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is collapsing the historical separation between statecraft and warcraft. This third volume of the series on Sovereign AI in the developing Global South examines how algorithmic systems are restructuring state authority in domestic governance and armed conflict. It first analyses "algorithmic statecraft": biometric digital public infrastructure and the risk of function creep, with India's Aadhaar and Kenya's Huduma Namba as cases, and predictive policing as a form of actuarial justice that can codify structural discrimination. The article then turns to "algorithmic warcraft": AI decision support systems used for target generation in Gaza, automation bias and the "triage trap" that hollow out meaningful human control, and bias in military AI. It traces the democratisation of lethality through commercial and AI-enabled drones in Myanmar, Sudan, Libya and the Sahel, Bangladesh's border-security modernisation in response to regional spillover, and generative AI as an instrument of cognitive warfare. It closes with the fractured diplomacy of the Global South in the UN Group of Governmental Experts on lethal autonomous weapons systems, and argues that sovereign resilience requires contextualised AI frameworks under strict civilian oversight together with a coordinated push for binding international norms.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Standard large language model (LLM) architectures process natural language sequentially using one-dimensional positional encodings and autoregressive causal masks. While effective for localized sequence generation, this serial pipeline creates severe processing bottlenecks during global structural synthesis, cross-modal translation, and parallel error detection. In contrast, neurodivergent human cognitive processing—specifically visual-spatial dyslexic architectures—treats textual and symbolic input as a two-dimensional spatial coordinate plane. Rather than relying on rigid, single-direction visual paths, this cognitive model deploys simultaneous multi-directional raster sweeps: horizontal (left-to-right, right-to-left), vertical (top-to-bottom, bottom-to-top), diagonal X-pattern scans, and dynamic mid-pass directional pivots upon semantic or structural convergence. This monograph formalizes Spatial-Matrix Attention (SMA), an artificial intelligence attention paradigm that replaces one-dimensional token queues with a 2D Euclidean coordinate tensor. By assigning spatial coordinates to tokens and enabling dynamic vector scanning with early-stopping pointer retrieval, SMA allows machine learning models to execute asynchronous parallel drafting, real-time self-proofreading, and low-latency ontological memory access without requiring heavy autoregressive re-evaluation passes. Main Highlights & Key Contributions: 2D Coordinate Embeddings: Replaces standard 1D sequential indexing with a dynamic 2D Euclidean spatial distance matrix and relative angular orientation tensors. Multi-Vector Matrix Rastering: Formalizes vertical column sweeps, cross-planar diagonal scans, and horizontal parsing for global layout and structural density verification. Mid-Sweep Directional Pivoting: Introduces stochastic angle switching and early stopping during raster passes when key semantic thresholds or structural anomalies are detected. Key-Bound Pointer Retrieval: Enables direct execution of pre-cached ontological macros, drastically reducing KV-cache expansion overhead during long-context reasoning.

This multi-volume monograph series introduces Spatial-Matrix Processing, a non-linear language comprehension framework that bridges human visuospatial cognition and next-generation artificial intelligence architecture. Moving beyond the rigid one-dimensional (1D) serial token processing of traditional autoregressive transformers, this work formalizes how language can be evaluated across a two-dimensional (2D) topological canvas. Inspired by the parallel scanning mechanics observed in visuospatial dyslexia—specifically multi-directional raster sweeps (X-pattern, diagonal, and inverse passes)—the framework demonstrates how semantic derivation can bypass sequential token queues in favor of key-bound spatial pointer retrieval. Volume I (Cognitive Architecture & System Blueprint) establishes the human cognitive foundations, contrasting 1D linear attention bottlenecks with 2D spatial-grid parsing. It outlines the architectural design for Spatial-Grid Attention (SGA) and real-time parallel compiling (simultaneous drafting and proofreading). Volume II (Mathematical & Thermodynamic Foundations) provides standalone mathematical rigor, deriving field-theoretic semantic emergence equations, pointer address collision probabilities (P_addr), dynamic resolution throttling algorithms (2D Spatial <-> 1D Linear fallback), and topological conservation under orthographic transposition. It presents the Zero-Entropy Error Transmutation Lemma, proving how structural disorder (such as letter transpositions) can be absorbed and transmuted into high-fidelity semantic intent without information loss.

While the practice of managing products to be delivered by means of large language models is growing rapidly and spreading, increasingly a new practitioner discourse is spreading in the field of product management. The PRD (Product Requirements Document), that for decades has been the core specification artifact of the function, would be replaced by the evaluation suite: a set of test cases scored by the evaluation environment of the product under development, the suite encoding in executable form what acceptable system behavior looks like. This simple statement is now almost a mantra in the practice of managing products, and so far has not been subject of any in-depth conceptual investigation. In the requirements engineering community for machine-learning-enabled systems, the challenges of specifying such systems have been analyzed in great detail, but this does not yet translate into practical artifacts and practices of requirements engineering that would be used by practitioners in industry. This paper attempts to specify in detail what is actually being replaced by the evaluation suite, and what corresponding problems and challenges are not addressed by the new artifact. The study is of a theoretical nature and builds on two streams of literature: requirements engineering for machine-learning-enabled systems, and measurement validity in artificial intelligence evaluation. First, we clarify that the PRD serves three separate purposes: defining requirements, coordinating stakeholders, and facilitating deliberation about product intent. We then argue that only the first of these functions is actually transferred to the evaluation suite. Next, we introduce the concept of specification residue, i.e. the portion of what has been specified that cannot be encoded in an executable form and therefore ends up in the black box of individual judgment. We identify three types of such residue. Finally, we introduce a contingency framework that specifies under which conditions of outcome measurability and process-constraint density eval-primary specification is appropriate. Our results indicate that executable specification may shift but not reduce the need for human product judgment, and, most importantly, that it removes the key artifact through which such judgment was previously recorded and contested.

Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

Vector quantization (VQ), in particular lattice-based methods, offer strong rate-distortion trade-offs for low-bit large language models (LLMs), yet their behavior under quantization-aware training (VQ-QAT) remains poorly understood. We scale lattice VQ-QAT to billion-parameter LLMs and multi-billion-token training regimes, and introduce SQuAT, a shape-gain VQ-QAT approach trained with a separate straight-through estimator (STE) for the shape and gain. SQuAT decomposes weights into direction and magnitude: normalized directions are quantized using an $E_8$-derived spherical codebook, while gains are quantized independently with low-bit scalar quantizers. We show that, unlike a standard STE applied to the full quantizer, which ignores the shape-gain structure, these separate STEs induce tangent-space updates for directions, yielding an implicit form of spherical (Riemannian) optimization. To enable scalability, we develop a distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment scheme, in which workers quantize disjoint weight blocks and communicate only discrete indices, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8$\times$ and allowing us to scale it to 10B tokens. Across instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen3-4B, and base Qwen3-1.7B, SQuAT consistently outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE under identical quantizers and initialization, and achieves SOTA VQ-QAT accuracy.

The lack of large, balanced, and shareable biomedical imaging datasets remains a major barrier to the development, validation, and clinical translation of artificial intelligence systems. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution, yet its real-world value critically depends on rigorous validation beyond visual realism. In this study, we present and systematically evaluate a stage-aware generative framework based on StyleGAN3 for high-fidelity biomedical image synthesis, using human embryo development in Assisted Reproductive Technology. The StyleGAN3 models are trained to synthesize embryo images at the Start of Blastulation and Blastocyst stages, using a curated cohort of 96 high-quality embryos (selected from an original set of 704 time-lapse IVF videos based on combined ICM/TE Gardner grades of AA, AB, or BA). To assess reliability and practical utility, we introduce a multi-level evaluation protocol integrating distributional similarity (Frechet Inception Distance), frequency-domain spectral analysis, and downstream task-based validation. Experimental results show that the proposed models accurately reproduce global morphological characteristics, with consistently higher fidelity and stability at earlier developmental stages (FID = 52.1), while later-stage synthesis is challenged by intrinsic data imbalance and heterogeneity. Spectral analysis reveals partial smoothing of high-frequency details, highlighting limitations not captured by conventional generative metrics alone. Importantly, downstream experiments comparing real, mixed real-synthetic, and fully synthetic evaluation scenarios using ResNet50 and EfficientNet-B0, with classifiers trained exclusively on real data in all cases, show that synthetic images remain discriminatively informative and occupy a structured, non-degenerate feature space consistent with the learned morphological patterns of the classifiers. Overall, this work provides an impact-oriented validation of synthetic biomedical imaging data and underscores the necessity of task-level evaluation as a prerequisite for the responsible use of generative models in ART and broader healthcare applications.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study investigated students’ engagement in Extensive Reading activities among English Education students at the University of Mataram. It aimed to describe students’ behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement and to identify the factors influencing their engagement. Although previous studies have reported the benefits of Extensive Reading for language proficiency and motivation, relatively little research has simultaneously examined the three engagement dimensions and their contextual influences in Indonesian EFL higher education. A qualitative descriptive design was employed with ten students completing a questionnaire and five students participating in semi-structured interviews. The closed-ended questionnaire functioned only as descriptive supporting data, while the semi-structured interviews provided the main qualitative explanations; therefore, the study was not designed as mixed methods and did not use inferential statistics. The questionnaire was used to identify general patterns through descriptive frequencies and percentages, while the interviews provided more detailed explanations of students’ reading experiences. The findings showed generally positive engagement. Behavioral engagement was reflected in relatively strong participation and effort, although reading consistency remained the main challenge. Emotional engagement was shown through interest, enjoyment, motivation, and positive attitudes toward English reading. Cognitive engagement appeared through reading strategies, comprehension monitoring, reflection, and connections between texts and prior knowledge. Five factors influenced engagement: reading materials and personal interest, language difficulty, time and academic responsibilities, motivation and academic requirements, and reading autonomy and lecturer support. Overall, students’ engagement in Extensive Reading was shaped by interacting personal, textual, and academic conditions.

In addition to the availability of machine translation technologies such as Google Translate, people now have the option of employing Generative AI to carry out the translation tasks. GenAI is capable of producing translations in any language in a quick and efficient manner. Students in English department who might be interested in pursuing careers as language translators in the future, should have mastered artificial intelligence technologies in order to thrive in the world that is always changing. The purpose of this study is to investigate the students’ perceptions regarding the employment of artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT for translating texts. This study was presented with two research questions, which are as follows: To what extent do students position AI translation tools in relation to human translation? When it comes to the employment of artificial intelligence for translation, what benefits and concerns shapes students’ attitude toward AI translation use? In order to collect the necessary information for this study, interviews were conducted with twenty-two students from English department at Binus University who were enrolled in Translation course. The interview transcripts were used as the data for this study, and they were analysed qualitatively using thematic analysis framework developed by Braun and Clarke (2006). There are three fundamental steps involved in doing thematic analysis. Starting with initial open coding, which involves classifying data into codes. The second step is grouping the similar codes and finally, defining and naming the themes for each group. Results show that five themes appear in this analysis. These are: conditional acceptance of AI translation, perceived advantages of AI translation, concerns about overdependence, human superiority in meaning, and ethical and institutional boundaries. The findings suggest that even though artificial intelligence translation is effective, it is still a limited tool that must continue to be controlled by humans.

Abstract Video surveillance systems have witnessed rapid advancements over the past two decades, fueled by progress in computer vision, artificial intelligence, and edge computing. However, despite extensive research, there remains a need for a review that synthesizes the architectures, methodologies, and evolving trends of intelligent video surveillance systems from a system-level perspective. Most existing literature reviews focus narrowly on individual tasks such as object detection, motion tracking, or anomaly recognition, without addressing how these components integrate within a complete system. This paper addresses this gap by conducting a systematic review of research published between January 2000 and July 2025, drawing from major digital repositories. The main contributions of this work are threefold: (1) it proposes a structured taxonomy of intelligent surveillance systems based on key functionalities, including object detection, motion tracking, abnormal event detection, vehicle and traffic monitoring, object counting, and multi-camera coordination; (2) it provides a comparative analysis of methodologies, datasets, and platforms used across studies; and (3) it explores the interconnections among these core tasks while identifying critical challenges such as real-time processing, privacy preservation, data scalability, and system interoperability. Key outcomes of this review include the identification of underexplored research areas—such as federated learning and cross-camera integration—and practical guidelines for designing next-generation surveillance systems. The literature analyzed was sourced from major digital repositories including IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, arXiv, Springer, and the ACM Digital Library.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human societies. In the many attempts to capture the novel trend of AI entering in all aspects of human life these days, hardly any research covers sustainability aspects of AI encroaching society. In the teaching of sustainability, AI appears as an way to improve carbon footprint as for energy savings opportunities – for instance by using online resources instead of physical books, reducing cognitive load of tedious tasks that had to be performed in educational settings previously, such as sifting through many books to find applicable cases in law school etc. At the same time, AI may create enormous environmental costs – e.g., through its electricity consumption use for big data storage and analytics – but also sustainability challenges – e.g., through eternally-living algorithms and technical devices. This chapter proposes weighing the costs and benefits of AI in sustainability education. In a Law & Economics analysis, the advantages and disadvantages of AI in sustainability education will be compared in order to present a framework to harvest the benefits but prepare for coping with the downsides of AI in sustainability education. Future student learning experience enhancement and educational changes due to AI in the future will be prospectively anticipated in the discussion. The future of education may positively develop in less cognitive load and diligent learning-by-heart but shift towards creative solution finding, navigating through a digital online jungle and development social network skills to find the right tools in a growing ocean of mushrooming AI advancements.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: The development of digital technology, artificial intelligence, environmental concerns, and changing workforce needs has encouraged organizations to adopt more sustainable approaches to talent management. This study aims to examine the development of sustainable talent management, identify its key practices, and analyze the role of digitalization, artificial intelligence, employee skill development, motivation, and retention in supporting organizational sustainability. This study employs a qualitative approach using a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) based on the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Relevant studies were identified through systematic searches of selected databases, screened according to predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria, and analyzed using content analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that sustainable talent management has evolved from a short-term, performance-oriented approach toward a more strategic and long-term perspective that emphasizes organizational sustainability and employee development. Its key practices include talent attraction and selection, competency development, employee motivation, and retention, supported by digital technologies and artificial intelligence. However, the implementation of these technologies requires continuous employee skill development and a human-centered approach to ensure that technological advancement remains aligned with employee and organizational needs. The study concludes that sustainable talent management integrates technological, human, social, and environmental aspects to support organizational sustainability and long-term organizational resilience.
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management

documents.abstract: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS's pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question-answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22%-33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4%-22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.

Nepali-English code-switched conversational speech presents severe challenges for automatic speech recognition (ASR), chiefly through script confusion (inappropriate mixing of Devanagari and Latin orthography) and elevated error rates at language switch points. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can adapt multilingual foundation models, but human code-switched audio is expensive to collect and annotate. We curate a new benchmark of 13,044 spontaneous podcast utterances (15.45 h total; 10,214 test, 2,830 dev), audited and verified to eliminate machine translation leakages and acoustic loops. We investigate a two-stage synthetic-to-real adaptation framework: Stage 1 applies SFT on 0.95 h of speech synthesized via a multi-speaker, dual-engine TTS pipeline; Stage 2 explores Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with transcription and script rewards. We find that synthetic SFT provides the primary cross-domain transfer to spontaneous human speech, reducing Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 23.40% to 21.52% (-1.88 pp) and switch-point error rate (SPER) from 35.89% to 28.77% (-7.12 pp). Subsequent GRPO yields small, statistically significant adjustments on 173 test utterances (1.69%), driving English script confusion (SCR_en) from 6.45% to 6.36% (p <= 0.001) and SPER to 28.70% (p = 0.022 clustered). Crucially, ablation reveals that in this SFT-converged encoder-decoder setting, an auxiliary script reward term yields performance identical to MER-only optimization because rollout candidate groups exhibit near-zero script variance on synthetic data. On monolingual benchmarks, SFT improves Nepali MER by 2.71 pp (stabilizing at 18.42% after GRPO, a 2.38 pp gain over baseline) while preserving English lexical WER (3.38% vs. 3.33%). Verified transcripts, timestamps, episode metadata, and reconstruction scripts are publicly released.

Code-switched (CS) automatic speech recognition (ASR) remains difficult because real CS speech is scarce and synthetic speech does not fully match it. We investigate whether synthetic CS speech is more useful for learning an adaptation-friendly initialization than for ordinary continual fine-tuning. We propose SyRA-CS, a pair-specific synthetic-to-real adaptation framework based on Reptile meta-learning. For each language pair and pretrained model, we meta-train on the corresponding synthetic CS-FLEURS subset and then adapt using one hour of labeled real target speech. We evaluate four architectural settings: Encoder-CTC, FastConformer-RNN-T, Attention Encoder-Decoder (AED) and Speech-LLM. Experiments cover on Arabic-, French-, German-, and Hindi-English, against synthetic-only transfer, real-only fine-tuning, and continual fine-tuning. SyRA-CS improves over continual fine-tuning on WER in all 16 model-pair comparisons and on CER in 15 of 16, with relative macro WER reductions of 17.7% for XLS-R and 5.3-5.8% for the other three models. The gains hold across the tested models but vary in size across architectures, language pairs and metrics.

Background: Nephron-sparing surgery has become a standard approach for localized renal masses because it preserves renal function while providing oncologic control comparable with radical nephrectomy. Robot-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) has expanded the minimally invasive management of increasingly complex renal tumors. This review summarizes contemporary clinical outcomes and emerging technologies in RAPN. Materials and Methods: A PRISMA-guided literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus for peer-reviewed English-language human studies published between January 2020 and June 2025. Search terms included robot-assisted partial nephrectomy, robotic partial nephrectomy, RAPN, nephron-sparing surgery, single-port robotics, augmented reality, three-dimensional surgical planning, fluorescence-guided nephrectomy, and learning curve. Manual reference screening was also performed. Twenty eligible studies were included for qualitative synthesis; quantitative meta-analysis was not performed because of heterogeneity in study designs and endpoints. Results: Comparative randomized, propensity-matched, and multicenter studies generally showed faster postoperative recovery, less pain, and shorter hospitalization with RAPN than with open partial nephrectomy, while maintaining comparable oncologic outcomes. RAPN was feasible for hilar, endophytic, and solitary-kidney tumors in experienced centers. Three-dimensional planning and augmented-reality guidance improved anatomical visualization and operative planning, while indocyanine-green near-infrared fluorescence supported selective ischemia and perfusion assessment. Single-port RAPN demonstrated broadly comparable perioperative outcomes with multiport approaches, although early adoption may involve longer operative times. Structured learning-curve and training models were associated with progressive improvement in operative performance and complication rates. Conclusion: Current evidence supports RAPN as a safe and effective nephron-sparing approach across a broad range of renal tumor complexity. Artificial intelligence-assisted image guidance, fluorescence-based perfusion assessment, three-dimensional planning, and next-generation single-port platforms may further improve precision and functional preservation. Larger multicenter randomized studies and longer follow-up are needed to establish durable oncologic, functional, and cost-effectiveness benchmarks.

We present the framework of TACS-RF - a Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave modules. In this framework, a large-language-model (LLM) coding agent (Claude Opus 4.8) directly drives industry-standard electronic-design-automation (EDA) tools such as Cadence Virtuoso/Spectre, Calibre, Cadence EMX, and Ansys HFSS to design RF and mmWave modules. We validate the framework through the agentic design of a 240-251 GHz sub-THz transmitter in a 90 nm SiGe BiCMOS process. The agent semi-autonomously designed the sub-blocks including a 60 GHz push-push Colpitts VCO with second-harmonic extraction, multistage differential cascode power drivers, a push-push frequency doubler, a differential bowtie antenna, and all the interstage matching networks. The transmitter chain with parasitic-extracted devices and EM-verified passives delivers +5.1 to +6.3 dBm across an 11 GHz varactor-only tuning range, phase noise of -80 to -88 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset while consuming a DC power of 361 mW. We describe the agent-driven design flow and the resulting division of labor between human and agent, taking a step toward a "text-to-ASIC" future for designing RF/mmWave hardware.

The article substantiates theoretical and pedagogical foundations for developing students’ positive attitudes towards inclusive education and professional motivation. It explains the interrelationship of inclusive awareness, value acceptance, empathy, professional self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, practical experience and reflection. A staged methodology based on cases, simulations, service learning, microteaching and reflective portfolios is proposed.
topics: Inclusion and Disability in Education and Sport

documents.abstract: In their lead article in Frontiers in Science, Boeringer et al. propose targeting networks of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) as a promising strategy for geroprotection (Boeringer et al. 2026). This approach builds on the remarkable versatility of GPCRs, which sense a wide range of extracellular signals, engage diverse signaling pathways, are broadly expressed across tissues, and play important roles in many disease processes. By framing the GPCRome as a central, druggable regulator of multiple hallmarks of aging, from inflammaging and mitochondrial dysfunction to stem cell depletion, the authors advance an intriguing hypothesis in which systems pharmacology could be used to rebalance several of these processes simultaneously, potentially delaying the onset of chronic disease and extending healthspan. The proposed integration of artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins, and quantum computing to rationally manipulate such complex signaling networks is bold and thought-provoking.At the same time, translating this compelling vision into therapeutic reality presents formidable biophysical, computational, and experimental challenges. The authors explicitly acknowledge several of these limitations, including the sparsity and variable quality of available training data, the context dependence of GPCR signaling, and, importantly, the fact that network-and AI-guided polypharmacology does not yet constitute a validated or generalizable framework for designing multi-receptor interventions. Several further considerations may help define what will be required to move this exciting concept from a compelling systems-level hypothesis toward an experimentally testable and ultimately translatable framework for GPCR network pharmacology.The proposed networks contain many receptors with established disease relevance, but deciding that a receptor belongs in an aging network does not tell us how it should be modulated. A therapeutic network requires knowing whether a receptor should be activated, inhibited, partially activated, allosterically modulated, biased toward one effector, or manipulated in a tissue-restricted manner, and by how much. This distinction matters because GPCR effects are strongly dependent on receptor density, coupling repertoire, accessory proteins, cellular state, ligand concentration, and tissue context.Especially problematic is the situation for biased ligands. Compared with binding data, efficacy data are sparse and functional measurements are not interchangeable across assays.A ligand that appears biased in one cellular background may not retain the same functional preference in another because receptor expression levels, membrane lipid composition, expression reserve, transducer abundance, signal amplification, and regulatory machinery differ. Consequently, pooling efficacy measurements from heterogenous assays may obscure the underlying pharmacology and limit the predictive utility of models trained on such data.The challenge, therefore, is not simply to assemble more data, but to assemble the right data, including their experimental context.The proposed GPCRome is necessarily constrained by measurements reported in the literature. This creates an important circularity: well-studied receptors become highly connected nodes, while poorly characterized receptors, including orphan receptors (i.e., receptors without known endogenous or synthetic ligands) or incompletely deorphanized GPCRs, may be absent or misrepresented despite mediating potentially important biology, leaving major blind spots in any GPCRome network reconstruction. Boeringer et al. also highlight receptors for which human or translational evidence remains limited, with several proposed nodes supported primarily by in vitro cellular assays and animal models. It remains uncertain whether network topologies derived from controlled rodent experiments will reproduce the networks operating in complex, heterogeneous human populations.A useful next step would therefore be a community-wide effort to construct a standardized, machine-readable GPCR functional atlas. But the harder question is what such an atlas should actually measure, as binding affinity alone is insufficient. Harmonized measurements of ligand association and dissociation, receptor expression and activation, G-protein coupling, β-arrestin engagement, pathway-specific efficacy, receptor trafficking and internalization, desensitization, and signaling duration, are urgently needed-ideally across multiple physiologically relevant cellular backgrounds. Rather than reducing heterogeneous experiments to a single activity label, negative results and experimental metadata should be collected as well, and ideally shared in standardized, accessible format. Such a resource could make network inference more robust and, importantly, reveal where uncertainty really lies. While ligands reshape populations of GPCR conformations, different transducers both select receptor states and undergo their own conformational changes. Thus, signaling cannot be reduced to a ligand-induced receptor state. Rather, AI-based structure prediction, molecular dynamics and enhanced sampling, structural biology, and biophysical measurements should be considered complementary approaches for characterizing receptor-transducer conformational ensembles (Wootten et al., 2013;Hilger et al., 2018).Kinetics adds another critical dimension. Ligand residence time, receptor activation and deactivation rates, trafficking and recycling, and the duration of downstream signaling may influence in vivo efficacy and therapeutic window beyond what is captured by equilibrium affinity or endpoint efficacy (Copeland et al., 2006). Incorporating these temporal features into network models could improve both the selection of network-level interventions and the prediction of physiological outcomes.Sparse data should not necessarily halt progress, but they should change the modeling strategy. Transfer learning offers a particularly attractive route: models can learn shared representations from data-rich GPCRs and then adapt to understudied receptors, provided that domain differences and uncertainty are explicitly modeled [e.g., (Provasi and Filizola, 2025)]. The goal should not be to manufacture confidence from sparse data, but to quantify uncertainty and use it to prioritize the next experiment. AI can then become an activelearning engine linking prediction to targeted measurements rather than a one-way generator of hypotheses (Nguyen et al., 2024).A related issue is chemical space. Much of the historical GPCR ligand repertoire was optimized for individual targets, not for deliberately engineered polypharmacology. The chemical matter already available to the field may therefore be a poor representation of the multitarget molecules needed for network control. While generative modeling architectures have successfully enabled the exploration of new regions of chemical space, the objective should be defined in terms of multi-receptor and multi-pathway pharmacology, including selectivity, efficacy, kinetics, tissue exposure, and safety, rather than simply potency at one receptor. This is where structure-based methods, functional profiling, generative chemistry, and experimental validation need to be tightly coupled.Perhaps the most important question is whether the proposed network architecture will have translational relevance. Boeringer et al. (Boeringer et al. 2026) present mechanistic hypotheses that draw largely on cellular studies, animal models, and selected examples of clinical pharmacology. However, networks inferred from preclinical systems may look quite different in patients, where age, genotype, comorbidities, medication history, tissue composition, and disease stage can all reshape signaling. The authors' vision of digital twins and patient-specific GPCR interventions is compelling precisely because it points to this missing layer.The next step should be to test these network hypotheses directly against patient-derived data rather than assume that preclinical networks represent stable therapeutic maps. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, proteomics, functional biomarkers, clinical phenotypes, and longitudinal treatment-response data could help establish which receptor nodes are conserved in humans and which are specific to particular tissues. Ultimately, the goal should not be to build a larger GPCR network, but a better-calibrated one that makes predictions that can be rigorously tested, challenged, and ultimately falsified in patients.A major strength of the Boeringer et al. article is that it challenges the field to think beyond the single receptor. That is an important conceptual shift. The next challenge is not simply to add more receptors, but to establish the experimental and computational standards needed to make network pharmacology genuinely testable. Such a program would: combine systematic, context-rich functional measurements with patient-derived evidence; use approaches such as transfer learning and uncertainty-aware active learning to deal with sparse data; account for receptor-transducer mechanisms and signaling kinetics rather than relying on static structures alone; and integrate physics-based and data-driven approaches to connect molecular mechanisms with cellular and organismal behavior (Hendrickx et al., 2020).The central question, then, is whether we can generate the data, assays, models, and chemical tools needed to perturb these networks in a predictable way. Turning this framework into something clinically useful will require considerably more experimental grounding and validation than the current computational roadmap implies.diseases might eventually become. But moving from theoretical network diagrams to clinically useful geroprotective therapeutics will require computational models firmly grounded in experimental biophysics and human biology. No single computational or experimental approach will be sufficient. What is needed instead is an integrated framework that brings together community-generated harmonized functional data, kinetic profiling, mechanistic modeling, generative chemistry, and patient-derived evidence. documents.abstract: Teachers’ occupational well-being is associated with their capacity to sustain effective teaching and support students’ academic engagement. This study aimed to determine teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement in select districts of Cagayan de Oro City Division during the School Year 2026–2027. The study described the respondents’ profiles, assessed their occupational well-being and student engagement, examined the relationships between these variables, and tested the moderating effect of the respondents’ profiles. It used a quantitative descriptive-correlational design involving two hundred and twenty (220) Grade 7 public secondary school teachers selected through universal sampling. Data were collected using a modified questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, Pearson Correlation, and multiple regression. Findings showed that job satisfaction was stronger than work-life balance, while workload stress was more pronounced than burnout. Emotional engagement emerged as the strongest dimension of students’ academic engagement. Job satisfaction and work-life balance were significantly related to student engagement. Workload stress showed no significant relationship, while burnout had a weak link only to emotional engagement. Class size and teaching experience affected these relationships, but the subject taught did not. The study concludes that teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement are interconnected, although their relationships vary across specific dimensions and profile characteristics. School administrators and teachers are encouraged to strengthen work-life balance, manage workload stress and burnout, promote cognitive engagement, and provide support responsive to class size and teaching experience.

Three-dimensional finite element analysis in geotechnical engineering is limited by two costs, the hours a direct solver spends factorising the stiffness matrix of a fine mesh and the hours an engineer spends building the model through a graphical interface. This paper presents Tellus3D, a geotechnical finite element program that attacks both costs together by treating a large language model (LLM) agent as its primary user and a rented graphics processing unit (GPU) as its primary solver, while the engineer’s role moves from operating the program to checking what the agent did. The program exposes 31 typed tools through the Model Context Protocol, so an agent builds the soil profile, structures, tunnels and construction phases, calculates, reads the results and writes a PDF report without a graphical interface, and the same project files open in a desktop application for review. The solver uses 10-node tetrahedra with Mohr–Coulomb, Hardening Soil, HS small and Soft Soil Creep models, an effective-stress undrained formulation, fully coupled Biot consolidation with Taylor–Hood elements, embedded piles, shells with zero-thickness interface elements, vertical drains with vacuum preloading, and staged tunnel boring machine (TBM) excavation with shield contraction. Its factorisation runs on an NVIDIA GPU through cuDSS in double precision, with a supernodal multifrontal Cholesky and a quasi-definite LDLT factorisation as the CPU fallback. On an RTX 4090 the factorisation of a 275,520-equation consolidation model took 3.7 s against 237–248 s on 25 CPU cores, which is a 64-fold speed- up, and the whole ten-year embankment analysis of 13 phases finished in 14.4 min, about 19 times faster than the estimated CPU time, because the stress updates remain on the CPU. A staged 6.6 m earth pressure balance tunnel drive of 17 phases in Bangkok clay solved in 225 s. Five instrumented case histories, calculated on an RTX 5090 in 2–15 min each with up to 918,914 equations, test the predictions: the model reproduces the 36 mm wall deflection of a 21 m Bangkok excavation within 4%, the trough of twin EPB tunnels after calibrating the shield contraction, and the final settlement of a vacuum-PVD trial at Suvarnabhumi within 7%, while it settles that trial too fast in the first six weeks, fails the Muar embankment about 1 m below the measured failure height, and moves a river wall of cement-admixed clay columns in stiff clay by about 6 mm against 42.6 mm measured. The analyses ran on a rented GPU costing about US$0.4 per hour, and the paper reports the verification and field benchmarks, the limits that the engineer must check, and why the remaining CPU work now bounds the speed-up.

The increasing adoption of generative AI presents new opportunities while raising AI governance and regulatory challenges, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) navigating the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). To support AI governance education, this study developed TESSA, a governance-oriented educational artifact within the OpenAI Custom GPT environment. Following a design science research approach, TESSA was evaluated against baseline ChatGPT using 100 benchmark scenarios through governance alignment assessment, human expert review, and consistency testing. Preliminary LLM-assisted assessment showed governance alignment rates of 90% for TESSA and 83% for baseline ChatGPT, while independent validation by an AI regulation law practitioner yielded 71% and 70%, respectively. Human expert review indicated that both systems provided generally strong governance guidance, while TESSA maintained high consistency across repeated executions. The findings suggest that governance-oriented grounding can support structured, practical, and stable AI-assisted compliance guidance for SMEs. The study contributes (i) a governance-oriented Custom GPT artifact for AI governance education, (ii) a human-validated regulatory update mechanism, and (iii) a multidimensional evaluation framework for governance-oriented AI artifact.

documents.abstract: Visual perception is often studied through the lens of object recognition. However, a large fraction of visual experience concerns image properties that are not naturally described in terms of discrete objects or categories. Visual textures provide a useful method to investigate this complementary aspect of vision, as they can be described through image statistics while spanning a wide range of perceptual and semantic complexity. In this thesis, I investigate how textures are represented in deep neural networks and humans, combining texture synthesis, representation analysis, computational modeling, and psychophysics. I first explored whether the naturalistic texture representations introduced by Gatys et al. (2015) could be combined with the latent space of a Variational Autoencoder to construct a controllable generative model of naturalistic textures. Although the complete model did not achieve the intended performance, the experiments isolated the texture representation proposed by Gatys as the most robust component of our framework and motivated a direct investigation of its representational properties. I then studied texture representations coded as Gram matrices across a diverse set of convolutional neural networks trained for object recognition. Texture information increased with network depth, but the resulting representations recovered only part of the categorical structure of natural textures defined by human judgment. Crucially, their quality was not correlated with measures of neural or behavioral alignment in object recognition. This dissociation indicates that being a good model of the ventral visual stream in an object recognition setting does not necessarily imply representing textures in a human-like way. Finally, I extended this analysis beyond convolutional architectures by comparing one CNN with three Vision Transformers across textures of progressively increasing complexity and with human performance in a psychophysical discrimination task. Vision Transformers formed substantially more consistent representations across texture types than the CNN, and these representational relationships were significantly better aligned with human perception. Taken together, these results show that texture perception provides a complementary benchmark for computational models of vision and exposes limitations within the dominant object recognition paradigm. More broadly, I suggest that understanding biological visual representations requires models and evaluation criteria that account not only for object identity and semantic content, but also for the statistical and contextual structure through which visual appearance is organized.

Purpose This study examined how speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety relate to second or foreign language (L2) learners’ willingness to communicate (WTC) in a GenAI-enhanced learning environment. More specifically, the study focused on the joint associations of these psycho-emotional variables with WTC and examined whether their alignment or discrepancy was related to learners’ communication willingness.Methodology A sample of 280 L2 learners completed measures of speaking self-efficacy, speaking anxiety, and WTC within a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-enhanced learning environment. Bivariate correlations were first examined to establish the associations among the variables. Response surface analysis (RSA) was then employed to examine the joint associations of speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety with WTC.Findings Speaking self-efficacy was positively associated with WTC, whereas speaking anxiety was negatively associated with WTC. The significant interaction between speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety indicated that their associations with WTC varied as a function of each other. The RSA showed that the direction of incongruence between speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety was systematically associated with WTC, with WTC higher when the discrepancy favored greater self-efficacy and lower anxiety. At the configuration level, the incongruent combination of high speaking self-efficacy and low speaking anxiety was associated with the highest WTC.Originality/value The study extends research on L2 learners’ WTC by moving beyond separate examinations of speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety and considering how these experiences operate in combination within a GenAI-enhanced instructional context.

The AI Courtroom: How Artificial Intelligence Is Reshaping Legal Practice explores the transformative role of artificial intelligence in the legal profession and the judicial system. The book examines how AI technologies are changing legal research, case analysis, contract drafting, evidence evaluation, litigation strategies, and courtroom administration. It highlights the opportunities offered by automation, predictive analytics, machine learning, and generative AI in improving efficiency, accuracy, and access to justice. At the same time, it critically addresses challenges related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, professional ethics, and the reliability of AI-generated legal information. The book also explores the evolving responsibilities of judges, lawyers, law firms, and legal institutions in an increasingly technology-driven environment. By connecting technological innovation with legal principles and judicial accountability, it provides valuable insights for law students, researchers, legal practitioners, policymakers, and technology professionals. Ultimately, the book emphasizes the importance of adopting AI responsibly while preserving human judgment, fairness, and the fundamental principles of justice.

Last month, leading executives of artificial intelligence (AI) companies warned the United Nations Security Council about the risks of losing human control over this rapidly advancing technology. Their recommendations focused heavily on safeguards, evaluation, and governance of AI models and systems, largely overlooking the risks that arise from the interactions of AI with people and institutions. AI safety needs to be addressed at the level of the human–AI system, not the AI model alone.

documents.abstract: Drawing from critical theoretical and empirical research, this study situates the Brussels Effect in HRM by problematising the processes of the globalisation of algorithmic workload management as a “regulatory mirage” of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act with its extraterritorial reach. The Act requires that high-risk HR systems be managed for risk, have human oversight, and be transparent; however, it does not provide for substantive worker dignity. The analysis shows a two-tiered global labour market based on the geography of the employer, with Global South workers at a disadvantage. The proposal made in this study is a Model Global Human Resource Artificial Intelligence Governance Protocol to bring the procedures into agreement with ethical justice.
